title: The tables below give information about sales of Fairtrade-labelled coffee and bananas in 1999 and 2004 in five European countries.
sampleText:
Model and sample answers for Writing tasks

TEST 2, WRITING TASK 1
MODEL ANSWER

This model has been prepared by an examiner as an example of a very good answer.
However, please note that this is just one example out of many possible approaches.

The two tables contain sales data for Fairtrade coffee and bananas in 1999 and
2004, in five nations of Europe.

The first table shows low-level coffee sales increasing in all five countries, albeit to
widely varying degrees. In two places sales increased by the same small amount:
1.8-2 million euros in Denmark, and 0.8—1 million in Sweden, The increment was
slightly larger in Belgium, from 1—1.7 million euros. Meanwhile, in Switzerland sales
doubled from 3-6 million euros. Finally, in the UK there was an enormous increase,
from 1.5-20 million euros.

In the second table, it is Switzerland which stands out as buying far more Fairtrade
bananas than the other four countries. Swiss sales figures jumped from 15-47
million euros across these five years, while in the UK and Belgium sales only

grew from 1—5.5 and from 0.6—4 million euros respectively. Sweden and Denmark

showed a different pattern, with falls in banana sales from 1.8-1 and 2-0.9 million
euros.

Comparing the two tables, it is clear that in 1999 Fairtrade coffee sales ranged from
0.8-3 million euros in these five countries, while banana sales also mostly clustered
between 0.6 and 2 million euros, with Switzerland the outlier at a huge 15 million
euros. By 2004, sales figures for both products had risen across the board, except
for Sweden and Demark which recorded drops in banana sales.

The pie chart below shows the main reasons why agricultural land becomes less productive. The table shows how these causes affected three regions of the world during the 1990s.

bullets.label: Worldwide: the three main causes (over-grazing, deforestation, over-cultivation)
Europe had the most degraded land
Oceania: over-grazing was the main problem
North America had the least degraded land

check.prompt: The pie chart below shows the main reasons why agricultural land becomes less productive. The table shows how these causes affected three regions of the world during the 1990s. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

phrases: The pie chart shows…, while the table compares…
Overall, … were responsible for the vast majority of…
…was the leading cause, accounting for…
…closely followed by…
…had the second-highest figure, at…
In contrast, only…% of land in… was degraded.
sampleText:
The pie chart shows the main causes of agricultural land degradation worldwide, while the table compares how three of these causes affected North America, Europe and Oceania in the 1990s.

Overall, over-grazing, deforestation and over-cultivation were responsible for the vast majority of land degradation, and Europe had by far the highest proportion of degraded land of the three regions.

Globally, over-grazing was the leading cause, accounting for 35% of degradation, closely followed by deforestation (30%) and over-cultivation (28%). Other factors made up the remaining 7%.

In Europe, 23% of land was degraded, mainly because of deforestation (9.8%) and over-cultivation (7.7%), with over-grazing contributing a further 5.5%. Oceania had the second-highest figure, at 13%, and here over-grazing was the main problem (11.3%), while over-cultivation had no effect at all. In contrast, only 5% of land in North America was degraded, with over-cultivation the most significant cause (3.3%) and deforestation having almost no impact (0.2%).

(About 180 words. It links the pie chart and the table, gives the global picture first, then compares the three regions from highest to lowest.)

title: The pie charts below show units of electricity production by fuel source in Australia and France in 1980 and 2000.

bullets.label: Total production rose in both countries
Australia came to depend on coal
France came to depend on nuclear power
Other sources (gas, oil, hydro) fell or stayed small

check.prompt: The pie charts below show units of electricity production by fuel source in Australia and France in 1980 and 2000. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

phrases: The pie charts illustrate the number of units of… generated from…
Overall, … rose considerably…, and by 2000 each country relied mainly on…
…half of which came from…
…had more than doubled to…
…from a much more balanced mix:…
…had increased dramatically to…, making up the vast majority of…
sampleText:
The pie charts illustrate the number of units of electricity generated from five fuel sources in Australia and France in 1980 and 2000.

Overall, electricity production rose considerably in both countries over the period, and by 2000 each country relied mainly on a single source: coal in Australia and nuclear power in France.

In 1980, Australia produced 100 units of electricity, half of which (50 units) came from coal. Natural gas and hydro power each provided 20 units, while oil accounted for 10. By 2000, total output had risen to 170 units, and coal-fired generation had more than doubled to 130 units. Hydro power also grew, to 36 units, but natural gas and oil fell sharply to just 2 units each. Nuclear power was not used in either year.

France generated 90 units in 1980 from a much more balanced mix: coal and natural gas produced 25 units each, oil 20, nuclear power 15 and hydro power 5. Twenty years later, however, nuclear power had increased dramatically to 126 units, making up the vast majority of production. Coal remained at 25 units and oil rose slightly to 25, whereas natural gas and hydro power dropped to only 2 units each.

(About 215 words. Note: the five figures in France's 2000 chart (126 + 25 + 25 + 2 + 2) add up to 180 units, not 170 as the chart title says, so the model avoids stating France's 2000 total.)

sampleText:
The pie charts illustrate how a UK school's yearly expenditure was divided between five categories in 1981, 1991 and 2001.

Overall, teachers' salaries were by far the largest expense in all three years, while insurance was always the smallest, although its share grew steadily.

In 1981, teachers' salaries accounted for 40% of spending, followed by other workers' salaries at 28%. Resources such as books and furniture and equipment each made up 15%, and insurance just 2%. Ten years later, the proportion spent on teachers' salaries had risen to half of the total, and resources had increased to 20%. By contrast, other workers' salaries fell to 22%, and spending on furniture and equipment dropped sharply to only 5%.

By 2001, teachers' salaries had decreased slightly to 45%, and other workers' salaries continued to fall, to 15%. Spending on resources also declined, to 9%. However, furniture and equipment rose dramatically to 23%, becoming the second-largest category, and insurance reached 8%, four times its 1981 level.

(About 185 words. It groups the changes by time period, highlights the biggest and smallest categories in the overview, and uses a range of verbs for rises and falls.)

sampleText:
The pie charts compare the age structure of the populations of Yemen and Italy in 2000, together with projections for 2050.

Overall, Yemen had a very young population in 2000, whereas Italy's population was considerably older. In both countries, the proportion of people aged 60 and over is expected to rise by 2050.

In 2000, half of Yemen's population (50.1%) was aged 0–14, while 46.3% were between 15 and 59, and only 3.6% were 60 or older. By 2050, the share of children is predicted to fall to 37%, and the working-age group is expected to grow to 57.3%. The proportion of elderly people will increase only slightly, to 5.7%.

Italy presents a very different picture. In 2000, the majority of Italians (61.6%) were aged 15–59, with 24.1% aged 60 or over and just 14.3% under 15. However, by 2050 the over-60s are projected to make up 42.3% of the population, not far below the 15–59 group (46.2%), while the proportion of children will drop further to 11.5%.

(About 190 words. Introduction (paraphrased), an overview with no numbers, then one paragraph per country with key figures and comparisons. No conclusion or opinion is needed.)

sampleText:
The three bar charts compare developing and industrialised countries in terms of average years of schooling, the number of scientists and technicians per 1,000 people, and spending on research and development (R&D) in 1980 and 1990.

Overall, industrialised countries were well ahead of developing countries in all three areas, and the gap between them widened over the decade.

In 1980, people in industrialised countries received an average of about 8.5 years of schooling, compared with only around 2.5 years in developing countries. By 1990, these figures had risen to roughly 10.5 and just over 3 years respectively. A similar pattern can be seen for scientists and technicians: industrialised nations had approximately 40 per 1,000 people in 1980, rising to about 70 in 1990, whereas developing countries increased only slightly, from around 10 to 15.

The most striking difference relates to spending on R&D. Industrialised countries spent approximately US$160 billion in 1980, and this more than doubled to around US$350 billion by 1990. In contrast, spending in developing countries actually fell, from about US$50 billion to roughly US$25 billion.

(About 200 words. It groups the three charts logically, gives an overview of the widening gap, and highlights the most striking change (R&D spending falling in developing countries while it doubled in industrialised ones).)

sampleText:
The bar chart compares the number of people in prison in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and Canada at ten-year intervals from 1930 to 1980.

Overall, the United States and Canada had the largest prison populations for most of the period, whereas Great Britain had the smallest figures at the start but saw a steady increase. By 1980, the US figure was by far the highest.

In 1930, Canada had the most prisoners, at about 120,000, followed by New Zealand and the United States, both at roughly 100,000. The US figure then fluctuated, peaking at around 130,000 in 1940 and falling to about 94,000 in 1970, before rising sharply to almost 140,000 in 1980. Canada's prison numbers followed a similar pattern but at a slightly lower level, ending at around 90,000.

In contrast, Great Britain had only about 30,000 prisoners in 1930 and 1940, but this number rose steadily to approximately 84,000 by 1980. New Zealand's figure dropped from 100,000 to just over 50,000 by 1950 and then climbed back to about 86,000. Australia's prison population fell from 70,000 to around 50,000, rose to 77,000 in 1970, and then fell again to 50,000 in 1980.

(About 230 words. The figures are read from the bars, so they are given as approximate (about, roughly, around). Note: the task says “table”, but the visual is a bar chart, so the model calls it a bar chart.)

sampleText:
The bar charts illustrate why students of different ages choose to study and how much support they get from their employers, in the form of time off and help with fees.

Overall, the younger a student is, the more likely they are to study for career reasons, while older students are mainly motivated by interest. Employer support is highest for the youngest group and lowest for students in their thirties.

Around 80% of students under 26 study for their career, compared with only 10% who study for interest. As age increases, the proportion studying for career purposes falls steadily, to 70% for those aged 26–29 and 58% for those in their thirties, whereas the figure for interest rises. The two reasons are equal at about 41% among 40–49-year-olds, and among students over 49, interest (70%) is far more important than career (just under 20%).

Turning to employer support, approximately 65% of students under 26 receive help, but this falls to around 51% for the 26–29 group and to a low of about 34% for those aged 30–39. After that, support increases slightly, reaching roughly 38% for students in their forties and 45% for the oldest group.

(About 220 words. It links age to the reason for study, uses “the younger…, the more…” for the overview, and points out the U-shaped pattern in employer support.)

sampleText:
The first bar chart shows the number of marriages and divorces in the USA every ten years from 1970 to 2000, while the second compares the marital status of American adults in 1970 and 2000.

Overall, the number of marriages fell over the period, while divorces peaked in 1980 before returning to their original level. In addition, a smaller proportion of adults were married in 2000, and more were divorced or had never married.

In 1970 and 1980, there were about 2.5 million marriages a year, but this figure fell slightly to 2.4 million in 1990 and then to 2 million in 2000. The number of divorces rose from 1 million in 1970 to a peak of about 1.4 million in 1980, before falling back to 1.1 million in 1990 and 1 million in 2000.

As for marital status, married people were by far the largest group in both years, although their share dropped from 70% to 60%. By contrast, the proportion of adults who had never married rose from around 15% to 20%, and the percentage of divorced people tripled, from about 3% to 9%. The figure for widowed adults remained fairly stable at around 7–8%.

(About 215 words. It describes both charts, uses millions for the first chart and percentages for the second, and highlights the biggest relative change (divorced adults tripling).)

sampleText:
The bar chart illustrates how many minutes of telephone calls were made in the UK each year between 1995 and 2002, broken down into local fixed-line calls, national and international fixed-line calls, and mobile calls.

Overall, local fixed-line calls were the most common type throughout the period, although they declined after 1999. In contrast, the other two categories grew continuously, with mobile calls showing the most dramatic increase.

In 1995, local calls accounted for about 72 billion minutes. This figure rose steadily to a peak of approximately 90 billion in 1999, but then fell back to around 72 billion in 2002, the same level as at the start of the period.

National and international calls increased every year, from roughly 37 billion minutes in 1995 to about 61 billion in 2002, which meant that by the end of the period they were only slightly below local calls. Mobile calls began from a very low base of just 3 billion minutes, but they grew slowly until 1999 and then rose sharply, reaching about 46 billion by 2002, more than fifteen times the 1995 figure.

(About 215 words. It groups the three categories by trend (rise-then-fall, steady rise, rapid rise) and supports each with figures from the start, the peak and the end.)
